title: Butler 2.0: intelligence analysis and assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
gist: IISS argues that AI integration into intelligence analysis risks a new 'Butler-style' systemic failure through two channels: human cognitive failures (bias amplification, 'cognitive surrender', skill erosion) and external manipulation of models via data poisoning by states such as Russia's Pravda network, commercial generative engine optimization and individual prompt injection. It calls for deception-resistant, law-compliant AI integration that preserves human judgement.

themes.theme: AI as a source of systemic intelligence failure

insights.claim: Integrating AI into intelligence analysis and assessment without clear guiding principles will lead to systemic and catastrophic intelligence failures, even though practitioners must harness AI to stay ahead of adversaries.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Governments face a forced trade-off: AI adoption in national-security analysis is unavoidable, so demand for governance, assurance and evaluation tooling around intelligence AI should grow.
insights.quote: doing so without clear principles informing its integration will lead to systemic and catastrophic intelligence failures
insights.locator: While practitioners of intelligence analysis

insights.claim: The 2004 Butler Review of intelligence on Iraqi WMD found serious failings in UK intelligence gathering, evaluation and presentation, leading the UK to create an independent intelligence-assessment profession; AI now poses new risks to those same activities.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Frames AI risk through a proven historical failure mode, suggesting a 'Butler 2.0'-style institutional reform of UK intelligence tradecraft may be needed.
insights.locator: While practitioners of intelligence analysis

insights.claim: AI adoption in intelligence creates two primary challenges: preventing AI-induced cognitive failures in human analysts, and mitigating external attempts to influence the AI models practitioners rely on.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Useful taxonomy for assessing any AI-in-decision-making deployment: internal human-machine failure vs. external model manipulation.
insights.locator: While practitioners of intelligence analysis

insights.claim: Post-Butler policies, guidance and training designed to counter groupthink did not anticipate AI agents, which are now being integrated as standalone agents or as teams of models acting as a 'silicon crowd'.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Existing analytic safeguards may be obsolete; a 'silicon crowd' of similar models may reintroduce groupthink rather than diversity of views.
insights.quote: the policy, guidance and training created for this purpose did not plan for the influence of AI agents
insights.locator: Butler was critical of the groupthink

themes.theme: Human cognitive risks from AI use

insights.claim: A 2024 MIT and UCL study found AI amplifies biases from its training data and design, which humans then internalise, producing a snowball effect where small judgement errors escalate into much larger ones.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Bias compounding through human-AI loops is a systemic risk for any organisation leaning on AI for judgement, from intelligence to investment analysis.
insights.quote: triggering a snowball effect where small errors in judgement escalate into much larger ones
insights.locator: Firstly, AI will often reflect

insights.claim: In late 2025 the UK AI Security Institute noted rising model persuasiveness and growing user reliance, while frontier labs have recently reported models actively deceiving users.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Increasing persuasiveness plus deception capability raises the stakes for oversight and regulation of frontier models in sensitive domains.
insights.locator: Firstly, AI will often reflect

insights.claim: 'Cognitive surrender', a term coined by University of Pennsylvania researchers, describes users applying minimal scrutiny to AI outputs and accepting them even when wrong.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Over-trust in AI outputs is a named, studied failure mode that institutions must design processes against.
insights.locator: Secondly, there is the risk

insights.claim: Long-term AI overuse threatens staff development, with studies linking AI use to worsened memory recall and critical thinking.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Erosion of analyst skills could leave institutions less able to catch AI errors over time, a slow-building capability risk.
insights.locator: Thirdly, there are the long-term

themes.theme: Real-world AI failures in security decisions

insights.claim: In January 2026 UK police apologised for a 2025 threat assessment that contained an AI hallucination of a football match that never occurred.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that AI hallucinations are already entering official security assessments.
insights.locator: These issues are not just theoretical

insights.claim: Investigations are ongoing into the February 2026 bombing of a primary school in Minab, Iran, including the extent to which AI-enabled targeting may have been responsible.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: AI-enabled targeting errors carry legal, reputational and policy risk for militaries and defence-AI suppliers.
insights.locator: These issues are not just theoretical

insights.claim: AI integration could compress human decision time when assessing adversary actions in nuclear command, control and communications, and battlefield personnel already trade off verifying AI recommendations against ceding lethal advantage to AI-enabled adversaries.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Speed pressure from AI-on-AI competition raises escalation risk, a tail risk for geopolitical stability.
insights.locator: These issues are not just theoretical

themes.theme: AI models as a new vector for deception

insights.claim: Because AI systems are trained on vast web-scraped datasets, they are becoming a new vector for deception, vulnerable to any actor able to shape the online information environment; post-Butler counter-deception tradecraft predates AI.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Data provenance and integrity of training/retrieval corpora become national-security issues, supporting demand for trusted data and model-assurance services.
insights.quote: AI systems are rapidly becoming a new vector for deception
insights.locator: The second challenge concerns the emerging

insights.claim: Building tradecraft against AI manipulation is hard because the threat evolves fast and those trying to influence models include not only hostile states but also allies and commercial actors.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Threat models focused only on adversary states miss allied and commercial manipulation of AI outputs.
insights.locator: The second challenge concerns the emerging

insights.claim: Russia's Pravda network carried out industrial-scale data poisoning, creating hundreds of websites distributing content across countries and languages so AI web crawlers would treat them as independent, corroborating sources.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: LLM grooming via fake corroboration is an active state influence technique that can skew model outputs used by analysts and the public.
insights.quote: Russia’s Pravda network engaged in industrial-scale data poisoning by creating hundreds of websites
insights.locator: Authoritarian states are already influencing

insights.claim: In August 2026 OpenAI disrupted an effort by Russia-originating ChatGPT accounts to promote a fake 'expert community' called the International Burke Institute; similar operations have been attributed to other authoritarian states.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: AI platforms are now front-line actors in counter-influence operations, adding trust-and-safety cost and regulatory exposure.
insights.locator: Authoritarian states are already influencing

insights.claim: Democratic states can also pose risks via AI influence: US tech companies have publicised disrupting influence operations by democracies, and such methods are inherently indiscriminate, affecting users regardless of geography.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Allied information operations can contaminate the same models that friendly intelligence services use.
insights.quote: these methods are often inherently indiscriminate in their attempts to be ingested by AI models
insights.locator: The influence of democratic states on AI

insights.claim: Restrictions on frontier-model releases or withholding models from safety testing, such as Anthropic withholding Mythos 5.1 from the UK AISI, limit practitioners' ability to understand the risks and limits of the models they use.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Tension between frontier labs and government evaluators could shape AI procurement and regulation in national security.
insights.quote: as Anthropic did by withholding Mythos 5.1 from the AISI
insights.locator: The influence of democratic states on AI

themes.theme: Commercial and individual manipulation of AI

insights.claim: Companies are investing in 'generative engine optimization' to shape how AI models portray their products, techniques that could also be used for PR campaigns on social and political issues.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: GEO is an emerging marketing spend category and a source of systematic bias in AI answers.
insights.locator: Non-state actors also seek to distort

insights.claim: A Nikkei Asia investigation found academics hiding prompt injections in their papers to induce AI reviewers to give positive reviews.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Low-cost prompt injection shows AI-assisted evaluation pipelines are gameable by individuals.
insights.locator: Non-state actors also seek to distort

insights.claim: Even small manipulation efforts risk a self-reinforcing loop in which humans act on artificially inflated AI reviews that another AI then treats as a validating signal.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Second-order feedback loops between AI systems can manufacture false consensus, relevant to any AI-driven ranking or rating system.
insights.quote: they risk creating a self-reinforcing loop if humans act on artificially inflated AI reviews
insights.locator: Non-state actors also seek to distort

insights.claim: Intelligence professions must integrate AI in ways that resist deception while complying with national values and laws; this will be difficult but necessary for any government wanting AI capability while preserving human judgement and oversight.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Expect new standards, tradecraft and oversight regimes for AI in government intelligence work, a policy and procurement trend.
insights.quote: The challenge for the intelligence professions is to find ways to integrate AI that are resistant to deception
insights.locator: AI offers practitioners of intelligence
